items.title: Report: Research Gold offers '100% human-written, never AI' medical research but uses AI-generated reviewers and unauthorized identities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Company Offering '100% Human-Written, Never AI' Medical Research Is 100% AI
items.summary:
Research Gold, a company claiming to provide fully human-written medical research services, including peer-reviewed manuscripts and systematic reviews, is using AI-generated profiles for its listed PhD reviewers and methodologists. Some real methodologists' identities and photos were used without their consent, and the company's communications, including phone and email interactions, are AI-driven despite claims of human expertise.

The company advertises adherence to established research standards like PRISMA 2020 and the Cochrane Handbook, but investigations found that key team members do not exist and have no online presence or publication history. After being contacted, Research Gold removed the unauthorized real individuals from its website. Attempts to verify the company's claimed contributions to published papers have not received responses from lead authors.

This revelation raises concerns about transparency and authenticity in outsourced medical research services, highlighting risks for researchers relying on such companies for critical academic work.

items.summary:
Google highlights that Go's design focuses on software engineering principles that support collaboration, maintainability, and long-term system evolution, which align well with AI-assisted coding workflows. The language's integrated toolchain, including formatting, testing, dependency management, and security features, helps both human developers and AI agents produce higher-quality, more reliable code.

Go's uniform ecosystem and standard library promote consistency across projects, enabling AI models to operate more efficiently and accurately on Go code. This structural coherence benefits teams managing large codebases and supports the evolving role of AI as a coding collaborator rather than a sole code writer.

items.title: Researchers decode hidden reasoning traces from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google LLM APIs, revealing thousands of leaked sensitive artifacts including API keys and passwords [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs
items.summary:
Researchers demonstrated that proprietary large language model APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google leak encrypted reasoning traces that can be decoded to reveal hidden tokens. By analyzing over 6,700 publicly available agent trajectories, they reconstructed more than 315,000 reasoning blocks containing sensitive information such as API keys, passwords, access tokens, and personal data.

The study found 704 distinct privacy artifacts, with 64 appearing exclusively in the hidden reasoning blocks and not in visible session data. This raises concerns about the confidentiality of user data processed by these models and highlights the need for improved security measures to prevent unintended information exposure.

items.title: Researchers find chain-of-thought prompting improves large language model reasoning on high-depth tasks but is redundant or harmful on shallow or intermediate tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Chain-of-Thought Helps and When It Hurts: An Empirical Investigation of the Serial-Depth Bottleneck in LLM Reasoning
items.summary: A study investigates the impact of chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting on large language model (LLM) reasoning, revealing that CoT helps overcome an architectural bottleneck related to serial computation exceeding a transformer's single-pass capacity. The research evaluates three instruction-tuned models across five NLP benchmarks, showing significant accuracy gains on complex, high-depth tasks like GSM8K and MATH, but minimal or negative effects on simpler tasks such as MMLU and ARC. The findings suggest CoT acts as a bandwidth bypass that aids tasks requiring extensive serial computation but offers little benefit for tasks that fit within the model's single-pass capacity.
items.description: A study investigates the impact of chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting on large language model (LLM) reasoning, revealing that CoT helps overcome an architectural bottleneck related to serial computation exceeding a transformer's single-pass capacity. The research evaluates three instruction-tuned models across five NLP benchmarks, showing significant accuracy gains on complex, high-depth tasks like GSM8K and MATH, but minimal or negative effects on simpler tasks such as MMLU and ARC. The findings suggest CoT acts as a bandwidth bypass that aids tasks requiring extensive serial computation but offers little benefit for tasks that fit within the model's single-pass capacity.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.09942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is widely assumed that chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting universally improves LLM reasoning. We investigate this through the conceptual framework of the H_dp bandwidth bound (Chen et al., 2024): although the formal bound binds only asymptotically (at astronomically large prompt lengths), it identifies a real architectural bottleneck -- serial computation exceeding a transformer's single-pass capacity must be externalised, which is what CoT does. Our central finding is a within-benchmark serial-depth gradient: single-pass (no-CoT) accuracy degrades monotonically with per-item serial depth, while CoT is approximately depth-invariant. We measure CoT effects across three instruction-tuned models (Qwen-2.5-7B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B) and five standard NLP benchmarks at practical context lengths. On high-depth P-complete tasks (GSM8K, MATH), CoT gives a +54 to +68 pp recovery gap across all models. On shallow TC^0 tasks (MMLU, ARC), CoT is structurally redundant (Delta in [0.0, +4.6] pp, no significant negative effect) -- though high no-CoT baselines (up to 95% on ARC) may reflect contamination, so this null is not a clean architectural test. The intermediate class L (HumanEval) shows a model-size-dependent transition: +23.2 pp (32B), +9.1 pp (8B), -28.7 pp (7B). The cross-benchmark depth-recovery correlation is Spearman rho = 0.661 (p = 0.007, n = 15); 9 of 15 benchmark-level McNemar tests are significant after Bonferroni correction. Pre-registered on OSF, our results indicate that CoT is not a universal reasoning enhancer but acts as a bandwidth bypass: it helps serial computation that strains single-pass capacity and is redundant for tasks that already fit.

items.title: Researchers identify procedural fairness failures in RLHF due to preference averaging, propose Preference-Aware RLHF to improve alignment accuracy and reduce fairness gaps [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Procedural Fairness Failures in RLHF from Preference Averaging
items.summary:
A new study finds that Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) often aggregates diverse human preferences into a single reward model, assuming homogeneity and causing majority preferences to dominate while minority views are under-represented. This leads to procedural fairness failures in alignment, where distinct preference signals are lost during reward modeling. The researchers introduce Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF), which separates optimization across different preference modes during reward learning, improving overall alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reducing fairness gaps between groups.

The work demonstrates that structural design choices in reward learning can cause fairness issues even in controlled, noise-free environments. These findings have direct implications for large language models and agentic systems, where biased reward models may exacerbate inequities across sequential decisions, highlighting the need for more nuanced approaches to preference aggregation in AI alignment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) aggregates heterogeneous preferences into a single reward model, assuming preference homogeneity. When preferences are heterogeneous, this aggregation induces a procedural fairness failure where majority preference groups dominate reward learning while minority preferences are systematically under-represented. This work defines procedural fairness in alignment as preserving distinct preference signals during reward modeling and shows that standard RLHF violates this via preference averaging. Preference-Aware RLHF (PA-RLHF) is introduced, separating optimization across preference modes at the reward learning stage. In a controlled setting, PA-RLHF improves overall alignment accuracy from 46.9% to 67.9% and reduces the fairness gap between best and worst aligned groups from 15.9 to 9.6 percentage points. These results show that procedural fairness failures in alignment can arise from structural design choices in reward learning, even in controlled, noise-free settings, with direct implications for large language models and agentic systems, where biased reward models can compound inequities across sequential decisions.

items.title: Riemann GeoResolver introduces a non-Euclidean attention framework extending inverse-distance attention from Euclidean to hyperbolic and spherical geometries with theoretical guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Riemann GeoResolver: A Non-Euclidean Attention Framework from Euclidean Resolver to Hyperbolic-Spherical Geometry
items.summary:
This paper presents the Riemann GeoResolver, a theoretical framework that generalizes inverse-distance attention from a Euclidean prototype to non-Euclidean settings using hyperbolic and spherical geometries. The authors prove three core theorems for the Euclidean case, demonstrating improved retrieval efficiency, convergence properties, and noise memorization limits compared to softmax attention. The framework then extends these results by replacing Euclidean distances with hyperbolic geodesic distances for memory storage and spherical geodesic distances for routing, integrating ten modules including curvature compression, gradient bounds, and sparse routing.

The work establishes a comprehensive theoretical foundation connecting Euclidean attention as a special case to more general hyperbolic memory and spherical retrieval mechanisms. The Euclidean theorems are fully proved, while analogous arguments support the non-Euclidean extensions, offering new insights into attention mechanisms across different geometric spaces.

The work establishes a comprehensive theoretical foundation connecting Euclidean attention as a special case to more general hyperbolic memory and spherical retrieval mechanisms. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10416v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a theoretical foundation for inverse-distance attention, from its Euclidean prototype (Resolver) to its non-Euclidean realization (Riemann GeoResolver). The Euclidean part establishes three core theorems: (1) circuit separation---IDA achieves exact retrieval with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ resources while softmax requires $\Omega((\log n)^2)$ width; (2) a Polyak--Lojasiewicz inequality with $\Omega(e^{\Delta^2/\sqrt{d}}/\Delta^2)$ stronger constant than softmax, implying linear convergence, $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ Lipschitz scaling under a low-rank/clustering assumption, $\Theta(1)$ Hessian spread, and absence of spurious local minima; (3) a width-independent effective rank bound that limits noise memorization---softmax memorizes arbitrary labels when $d_h\ge n$, while IDA limits test error to $\mathcal{O}(\eta^2)$. The non-Euclidean extension then builds upon this prototype, replacing Euclidean distance with hyperbolic geodesic distance for storage and spherical geodesic distance for routing. The Riemann GeoResolver framework comprises ten integrated modules: four HIDA operators spanning $\Theta(n^2)$ to $\Theta(1)$ per token; Hyperbolic Curvature Compression (HCC) with provable error bounds; HyperGate with gradient lower-bound theorem; Spherical Inverse Distance Attention (SIDA) with sphere-analog PL inequalities; Dynamic Memory Genesis (DMG) with $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ regret bounds; and Geodesic Sparse Routing (GSR) with quality and communication bounds. The Euclidean theorems are proved in full; the non-Euclidean extension theorems are proved with analogous arguments. This work establishes a theoretical arc: from Euclidean attention as a special case, to hyperbolic memory, to spherical retrieval.

The framework then extends these results by replacing Euclidean distances with hyperbolic geodesic distances for memory storage and spherical geodesic distances for routing, integrating ten modules including curvature compression, gradient bounds, and sparse routing.

The work establishes a comprehensive theoretical foundation connecting Euclidean attention as a special case to more general hyperbolic memory and spherical retrieval mechanisms. The Euclidean theorems are fully proved, while analogous arguments support the non-Euclidean extensions, offering new insights into attention mechanisms across different geometric spaces.

items.title: Researchers propose cost-aware cross-tier transfer method for evolutionary optimization of LLM prompts, reducing search costs by up to 54x while maintaining performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimize Cheap, Deploy Strong: Cost-Aware Cross-Tier Transfer for Evolutionary Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers present a method to optimize large language model (LLM) prompts and agentic programs by decoupling LLM roles and running high-volume answering on cheaper tiers, reserving stronger models for rare reflection and variation steps. This approach enables upward cross-tier transfer, deploying cheaply evolved prompts on stronger target models, significantly lowering search costs.

The study evaluates this method across four tasks and eleven models from four families, showing that it matches or exceeds same-tier optimization while using over 96% of search tokens on the cheapest tier. Cost reductions range from 5.6 to 14 times, increasing to 25 to 54 times when reasoning tiers generate long chains of thought during fitness evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolutionary optimization of LLM prompts and agentic programs (e.g., GEPA) is dominated by fitness evaluation: scoring each candidate runs an answering LLM over a validation set, so the evaluator's price tier dictates total search cost. We restructure that search by decoupling the three roles an LLM plays, running the high-volume answering role on the cheapest tier, reserving a strong model for the rare reflection/variation operator, then exploiting upward cross-tier transfer to deploy the cheaply evolved prompt on a stronger target. We contribute a cost-controlled characterization of when cheap-tier search substitutes for target-tier search, and where it fails. Across four tasks (HotpotQA, IFBench, LiveBench-Math, HoVer) and eleven models in four model families, the resulting prompt matches or exceeds same-tier optimization while placing over 96% of search tokens on the cheapest tier, at 5.6-14x lower search cost, rising to 25-54x where reasoning tiers emit long chains of thought on every fitness call.

items.originalTitle: Your LLM, Your Style: Behavioral Mode Axes for LLM Behavioral Control
items.summary: Researchers present a situated behavioral-data framework to study and control large language model (LLM) behavioral personalities, using 3,200 contrastive scenarios covering 20 behavioral patterns and four prompt registers based on validated psychometric facets. They find that LLMs exhibit stable, model-specific behavioral profiles with register-dependent shifts in decisions, advice-giving, and task execution. The study introduces Behavioral Mode Axes (BMAs), activation-space directions derived from behavioral traces, to control these patterns more effectively, with thought-derived BMAs providing cleaner control than response-derived ones. This approach suggests LLM personality-like tendencies are better understood as measurable and controllable behavioral modes grounded in interaction contexts rather than abstract self-report traits.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act in interactive settings where their behavioral styles affect user experience, safety, and downstream decision making. Existing LLM personality studies largely rely on self-report questionnaires administered in first-person settings, making the resulting profiles sensitive to surface elicitation choices and poorly grounded in concrete model behavior. In this work, we introduce a situated behavioral-data (B-data) framework for studying and controlling LLM behavioral personality. We construct 3,200 contrastive behavioral scenarios spanning 20 behavioral patterns and four prompt registers, grounded in validated psychometric facets such as BFI-2, DOSPERT, and HEXACO. Using this framework, we find that LLMs exhibit stable and model-specific behavioral profiles, while also revealing register-dependent shifts across first-person decisions, advice-giving, and task execution. We then show that these behavioral patterns can be controlled through Behavioral Mode Axes (BMAs), activation-space directions derived from contrastive behavioral traces. Compared with response-derived BMAs, which are more prone to trait drift, thought-derived BMAs more faithfully capture the intended behavioral mechanism and provide cleaner control over situated behavioral styles. Our results suggest that LLM personality-like tendencies are better understood not as abstract self-report traits, but as measurable and controllable behavioral modes grounded in concrete interaction contexts. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/lhz191/LLM-Behavioral-Personality.

items.title: Researchers introduce ConVAWG, a retrieval-grounded framework generating controlled synthetic multi-turn dialogues modeling Violence Against Women and Girls scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ConVAWG: A Retrieval-Grounded Framework for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation in Violence Against Women and Girls
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ConVAWG, a framework designed to generate synthetic multi-turn dialogues that model conversational dynamics in Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios. The system builds scenarios using persona seeds, demographic data from the UK Office for National Statistics, official crime definitions, and Domestic Homicide Review cases, converting these into hierarchical event timelines and role-play dialogues with targeted toxicity control.

ConVAWG addresses challenges in accessing and annotating real conversation data in sensitive domains by releasing over 6,000 dialogue events across 200 scenarios with detailed metadata. Evaluations including human assessments and large language model judgments demonstrate strong dialogue quality and fidelity to the domain, supporting research into relational and temporally unfolding abuse phenomena beyond sentence-level toxicity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthetic dialogue generation offers a way to study conversational dynamics in sensitive domains where real data are difficult to access, release, or annotate. The underlying abuse may occur online or offline: threats and coercion can appear directly in messages, while behaviours such as surveillance, isolation, stalking, and physical violence may be planned, disclosed, or referred to conversationally. Privacy and legal constraints make it difficult the release of large-scale real conversation datasets; existing work has mostly focused on sentence-level toxicity of online abuses, leaving a gap in modelling abuse as a relational and temporally unfolding phenomenon. In this work, we focus on modelling Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios as multi-turn dialogues. We introduce ConVAWG, a retrieval-grounded framework for generating CPS-aligned synthetic VAWG chat dialogues. ConVAWG builds scenarios from persona seeds, demographic patterns reported by the UK Office for National Statistics, official crime definitions, and retrieved Domestic Homicide Review cases; converts them into hierarchical event timelines; generates multi-scene role-play dialogues; and applies targeted activation-steered toxicity control to appropriate utterances. We release over 6,000 multi-turn dialogue events across 200 scenarios with rich scenario-, event-, and turn-level metadata. Extensive human evaluation, LLM-as-Judge assessment, ablations, and downstream tasks show strong dialogue quality and domain fidelity.

items.title: AXIOM launches a trust-first neuro-symbolic system for natural-language mathematical reasoning with 90% accuracy and self-explaining step traces [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AXIOM: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary:
AXIOM is a neuro-symbolic architecture that converts informal math problems into a structured schema processed by a deterministic computer algebra system (CAS) to derive and verify answers or abstain. It uses a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompts, and CAS handlers, with 4,783 routes deployed, 71% answering without invoking the language model, and no regressions in correctness.

On the MATH test set, AXIOM achieves 90.2% accuracy with one confident wrong answer, and on held-out MATH-500 data, it scores 89.2% with zero confident wrong answers, demonstrating robustness beyond memorization. The system also answers a 20,000-record arithmetic benchmark at 100% accuracy in 1 ms per record and has served approximately 30,000 public queries.

AXIOM emphasizes trustworthiness by treating abstentions as first-class outputs and enabling continuous improvement without regressions, applying disciplined methods like math-template bucketing and regression scanning. This approach aims to extend trustworthy neuro-symbolic reasoning beyond mathematics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.00671v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present AXIOM, a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for natural-language mathematical reasoning. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives and verifies the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment between problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form CAS handler, with 4,783 such routes shipped, 71% of which answer without invoking the language model, and zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived rather than generated, so is its explanation: every handler emits a step trace of the computation it performed, rendered as prose by a layer covering all 4,785 tasks that cannot narrate a step the handler did not take. We report two numbers and never fuse them. On the full 7-category MATH test split, designed against, AXIOM answers 90.2% correctly (4,510/5,000) with one confident-wrong answer (99.98% trust on parseable). On held-out MATH-500, never designed against, it answers 89.2% correctly (446/500) with zero confident-wrong answers. The 1.0 pp gap is the substantive result: a registry that had merely memorized problem shapes would collapse on held-out data, and this one does not. The rule-only path answers the 20,000-record lm-eval arithmetic benchmark at 100% in 1 ms per record; the system has served ~30,000 public queries. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry. The discipline behind it (math-template bucketing, LOST_CORRECT scan as regression oracle, parseable-first onboarding, abstain as first-class output) transfers to trustworthy neuro-symbolic systems beyond mathematics.

items.title: Researchers train probes on LLM pre-generation activations to predict success on math and coding tasks, enabling up to 70% inference cost reduction by routing queries across models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LLMs Encode Their Failures: Predicting Success from Pre-Generation Activations
items.summary:
Researchers investigated whether large language models (LLMs) encode their likelihood of success in internal representations before generating outputs, aiming to improve inference efficiency. They trained linear probes on pre-generation activations to predict task-specific success, outperforming surface features like question length, and demonstrated that models encode a notion of difficulty distinct from human difficulty, especially with extended reasoning.

Using the E2H-AMC dataset, which includes both human and model performance on identical problems, the team showed that leveraging these probes to route queries across multiple models can surpass the best single model's performance while reducing inference costs by up to 70% on math tasks. This approach highlights how internal model representations can guide more efficient computation even when they diverge from human intuitions about problem difficulty.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.09924v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Running LLMs with extended reasoning on every problem is expensive, but determining which inputs actually require additional compute remains challenging. We investigate whether their own likelihood of success is recoverable from their internal representations before generation, and if this signal can guide more efficient inference. We train linear probes on pre-generation activations to predict policy-specific success on math and coding tasks, substantially outperforming surface features such as question length and TF-IDF. Using E2H-AMC, which provides both human and model performance on identical problems, we show that models encode a model-specific notion of difficulty that is distinct from human difficulty, and that this distinction increases with extended reasoning. Leveraging these probes, we demonstrate that routing queries across a pool of models can exceed the best-performing model whilst reducing inference cost by up to 70\% on MATH, showing that internal representations enable practical efficiency gains even when they diverge from human intuitions about difficulty. Our code is available at: https://github.com/KabakaWilliam/llms_know_difficulty

items.originalTitle: Loop, Think, & Generalize: Implicit Reasoning in Recurrent-Depth Transformers
items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.07822v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study implicit reasoning, i.e. the ability to combine knowledge or rules within a single forward pass. While transformer-based large language models store substantial factual knowledge and rules, they often fail to compose this knowledge for implicit multi-hop reasoning, suggesting a lack of compositional generalization over their parametric knowledge. To address this limitation, we study recurrent-depth transformers, which enables iterative computation over the same transformer layers. We investigate two compositional generalization challenges under the implicit reasoning scenario: systematic generalization, i.e. combining knowledge that is never used for compositions during training, and depth extrapolation, i.e. generalizing from limited reasoning depth (e.g. training on up to 5-hop) to deeper compositions (e.g. 10-hop). Through controlled studies with models trained from scratch, we show that while vanilla transformers struggle with both generalization challenges, recurrent-depth transformers can effectively make such generalization. For systematic generalization, we find that this ability emerges through a three-stage grokking process, transitioning from memorization to in-distribution generalization and finally to systematic generalization, supported by mechanistic analysis. For depth extrapolation, we show that generalization beyond training depth can be unlocked by scaling inference-time recurrence, with more iterations enabling deeper reasoning. We further study how training strategies affect extrapolation, providing guidance on training recurrent-depth transformers, and identify a key limitation, overthinking, where excessive recurrence degrades predictions and limits generalization to very deep compositions.

items.title: Researchers propose L2C framework for causal discovery with latent variables, learning cluster structure from local causal patterns without manual mapping [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Local to Cluster: A Unified Framework for Causal Discovery with Latent Variables
items.summary: The L2C (Local to Cluster Causal Abstraction) framework addresses challenges in causal discovery posed by latent variables and unknown cluster assignments. It learns cluster structures from local causal patterns and represents each cluster with up to three micro-variables, enabling macro-level causal reasoning without prior cluster knowledge. The method uses local discovery on maximal ancestral graphs to identify direct causes, effects, and V-structures, followed by cluster-level inference through a specialized calculus. L2C is sound, complete, and computationally efficient, connecting micro-level information to macro causal effects in complex settings where latent variables are unavoidable.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.22416v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent variables pose a fundamental obstacle to both causal discovery and inference. Local approaches exploiting direct neighborhood relations provide little beyond immediate dependencies. Cluster-level methods, though capable of broader reasoning, generally require cluster assignments or causal sufficiency in advance, conditions that are rarely satisfied in practice. Applying single-variable discovery at cluster resolution violates these conditions and thereby produces systematic bias. L2C (Local to Cluster Causal Abstraction) learns cluster structure from local causal patterns without manual variable-to-cluster mapping. The framework rests on a cluster reduction theorem: each cluster can be represented by at most three micro-variables, with no loss of macro-level identifiability. In the presence of latent variables, local discovery on maximal ancestral graphs recovers direct causes, effects, and V-structures, followed by cluster-level inference through a corresponding calculus on the resulting graph. Macro causal effects are formulated as joint interventions on the micro-variables within each target cluster. The framework is sound, atomically complete, and polynomially bounded. L2C establishes a direct connection from local micro-level information to macro causal reasoning in settings where clusters are unknown and latent variables are unavoidable.

items.title: Researchers propose stage-wise preference optimization with hard examples to reduce hallucination in multimodal large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Grounded Post-Training with Hard Examples for Reducing Hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers address hallucination in vision-language models, where generated responses may be linguistically plausible but visually inconsistent, by introducing a stage-wise preference optimization framework that constructs targeted multimodal data near known failure boundaries. Their approach focuses on ambiguous spatial orientation, object relationships, OCR uncertainty, and adversarial false-premise training to improve grounding consistency and reduce hallucination.

Experiments on open-source benchmarks and real-world scenarios demonstrate that this method produces more visually grounded and informative responses compared to several leading proprietary models. The findings suggest hallucination arises not only from limited model capacity but also from autoregressive generation's tendency to favor plausible linguistic continuations under weak visual grounding, indicating future research directions in physical consistency modeling and uncertainty-aware multimodal reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.16411v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hallucination remains a fundamental challenge in vision-language models (VLMs), where autoregressive generation may produce linguistically plausible yet physically inconsistent or visually ungrounded responses due to likelihood maximization under joint probabilistic modeling. We propose a stage-wise preference optimization framework for hallucination reduction through targeted multimodal data construction. Rather than directly optimizing on generic instruction-following data, our approach progressively constructs hallucination-focused preference pairs near known failure boundaries. The framework emphasizes ambiguous spatial orientation, object relationships, OCR uncertainty, and adversarial false-premise training. Hallucinated negatives are generated through minimally perturbed yet visually inconsistent alternatives, enabling Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to better separate grounded reasoning from plausible hallucination. Experiments on open-source benchmarks and real-world multimodal evaluation scenarios demonstrate improved grounding consistency, reduced hallucination, and more informative grounded responses. Cross-model qualitative evaluation further shows that the proposed multimodal LLM DPO framework produces more visually grounded responses than several frontier proprietary VLMs, such as in ambiguous spatial reasoning and adversarial false-premise settings. The results suggest that hallucination may arise not only from limited model capacity, but also from inherent tendencies of autoregressive probabilistic generation to favor linguistically plausible continuations under weak visual grounding. Future work may explore physical consistency modeling, uncertainty-aware multimodal reasoning, and architectural alternatives beyond standard autoregressive decoding.

items.title: Researchers introduce a Multi-Group Item Response Theory model to analyze safety degradation in large language models across 10 languages, revealing language-specific vulnerabilities and mistranslation impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Do Safety Guardrails Degrade Across Languages?
items.summary:
Researchers developed a Multi-Group Item Response Theory (IRT) framework to disentangle factors affecting safety degradation in large language models across multiple languages. Evaluating 61 model configurations on 1.9 million responses from 10 languages, they found that safety failures are primarily driven by a shared mechanism but vary by language and prompt type, with some models more vulnerable in English than in low-resource languages. The study highlights that mistranslations and cultural mismatches contribute to safety gaps, especially in physical harm categories like theft and weapons.

The IRT framework outperforms traditional metrics by accurately predicting safety vulnerabilities even when entire languages are excluded from training data. This approach enables fairer cross-lingual safety evaluation and suggests targeted improvements in dataset construction to address concept-language mismatches and reduce safety risks in multilingual AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.17173v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models exhibit safety degradation in non-English languages. Standard evaluation relies on Jailbreak Success Rate (JSR), which confounds several safety-driving factors into one, obscuring the specific cause(s) of safety failure. We introduce a latent variable model, a Multi-Group Item Response Theory (IRT) framework, that decouples language-agnostic safety robustness ($\theta$), intrinsic prompt hardness ($\beta$), global language processing difficulty ($\gamma$), and a prompt-specific cross-lingual safety gap ($\tau$). Using the MultiJail dataset, we evaluate the safety robustness of 61 model configurations across 5 closed-model families and 10 languages of varying resource, aggregating a dataset of 1.9 million responses. Exploratory Factor Analysis shows safety is primarily unidimensional: models refuse different harm types mainly through a shared mechanism. Contrary to the expected trend that safety degrades largely in low-resource languages, 22 model configurations are more vulnerable in English than in low-resource languages. Low-resource languages produce more uncertain responses (high entropy) than high-resource languages. Also, high-$\tau$ prompts cluster in physical harm categories like Theft and Weapons and lower-resource languages, trends validated through cross-dataset generalization. While global translation quality shows low correlation with $\tau$, severe mistranslations drive high-bias outliers, as validated by native speakers. Cultural and conceptual grounding mismatches may also contribute to $\tau$. In predictive validation, the IRT framework achieves $\mathrm{AUC} = 0.940$, and unlike rate baselines stays predictive when a whole language is held out ($0.875$). Our framework reveals concept-language vulnerabilities that aggregate metrics obscure, enabling fairer cross-lingual safety evaluation and targeted improvements in dataset construction.

items.title: Researchers find context-truthfulness is preserved across large language model lineages and propose TruthProbe to enhance truthful attention heads [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Truth Stays in the Family: Enhancing Contextual Grounding via Inherited Truthful Heads in Model Lineages
items.summary:
Researchers investigated whether foundational large language models (LLMs) and their specialized multimodal variants (MLLMs) share behavioral traits related to context-truthfulness. They quantified truthfulness at the attention-head level across diverse model families including Vicuna, Qwen2.5, LLaMA2, and Mistral, finding that truth scores are strongly preserved within lineages even after instruction tuning or multimodal adaptation. This preservation aligns with attention-head weight retention, with truthful heads focusing on query-relevant evidence.

Building on these findings, the team introduced TruthProbe, a soft-gating method that amplifies context-truthful heads while maintaining other head contributions. TruthProbe improved contextual truthfulness on benchmarks like HaluEval and reduced multimodal hallucinations on POPE and CHAIR datasets. The approach leverages the inheritance of truthfulness from base LLMs to their fine-tuned descendants, and the researchers have made their code publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.15821v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have produced many specialized multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) that share common foundational LLMs, forming distinct model lineages. It remains unclear whether a fundamental behavioral link exists between the foundational LLMs and downstream variants. We investigate this question by quantifying head-level context-truthfulness scores. Across diverse LLM and MLLM lineages, including Vicuna-, Qwen2.5-, LLaMA2-, and Mistral-based models, we find that Truth Scores are strongly preserved within model families, even after instruction tuning or multimodal adaptation. We further show that this inheritance is consistent with attention-head weight preservation, and that context-truthful heads attend to query-relevant evidence. Building on this finding, we propose TruthProbe, a soft-gating strategy that amplifies context-truthful heads while preserving other head contributions. TruthProbe improves contextual truthfulness on HaluEval and reduces multimodal hallucination on POPE and CHAIR, with base-LLM Truth Scores transferring effectively to their fine-tuned LLM and MLLM descendants. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/TruthProbe.

items.title: Researchers identify and correct structural-role bias in KV cache eviction for long-context LLMs, improving accuracy on schema-dense inputs like nested JSON [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptive Filtering of the KV Cache: Diagnosing and Correcting Structural-Role Bias in LLM Inference
items.summary: Researchers analyzed attention-based KV cache eviction methods used in long-context language models and found that these methods disproportionately retain non-content tokens such as delimiters and structural keys, which degrade exact-match accuracy significantly under tight memory budgets. They demonstrated that suppressing structural key tokens during cache eviction improves signal-to-noise ratio and accuracy, especially at low memory budgets. The team introduced a retraining-free, role-conditional allocation method over existing scoring mechanisms, which recovers most of the accuracy loss without additional training and incurs negligible inference cost using a small linear role probe. While this approach closes much of the performance gap, matching parser-level downstream accuracy remains an open challenge.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.13205v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Attention-based KV cache eviction (H2O and its descendants) compresses the memory-constrained state of a long-context model by ranking tokens on accumulated attention mass, treated here as signal energy, and keeping the heaviest. On schema-dense input streams such as nested JSON, this score acts as a non-stationary filter that disproportionately retains noise: a non-content sink role (delimiters or whitespace) carries an order of magnitude more energy than any content role, and structural KEY tokens are over-retained at roughly 1.8x the rate of the answer-carrying VALUE tokens, collapsing exact-match accuracy from 88% to 0% at a 5% budget as the signal-to-noise ratio of the retained state degrades. A counterfactual experiment establishes that suppressing KEY tokens is the best deployable filter. Our retraining-free, role-conditional allocation over SnapKV's windowed score, governed by a single tuned hyperparameter, closes 63-98% of the H2O gap at sub-20% budgets and, at higher budgets, modestly matches or exceeds full-cache accuracy -- a small, seed-sensitive denoising effect (borderline significant at B=0.50; not distinguishable from zero at B=0.30 over four seeds). A 15 MB linear role probe supplies these labels at negligible inference cost, though matching parser-level downstream accuracy remains open.

items.title: Researchers analyze converting large pretrained transformers to smaller models, finding representation alignment but weak parameter alignment and proposing initialization-based conversion methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wiring Beats Blending: What Transfers Between Transformer Sizes -- and What Doesn't
items.summary: Researchers studied the conversion of a 1.4 billion parameter transformer model to a smaller 410 million parameter sibling within the Pythia family, finding strong alignment in representations but weak alignment in parameters. They showed that dense weight projection disrupts key model structures and that the value of conversion lies primarily in initialization rather than direct weight transfer. The team decomposed conversion into two independent methods: least-squares compensation, which improves zero-shot performance efficiently, and variance-preserving rescaling, which benefits endpoint performance after continued pre-training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.02829v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model families are typically trained size by size, each from scratch. Can apretrained large model instead be converted into a smaller sibling? Wecharacterize the 1.4B->410M conversion in the Pythia family end to end.Representations align strongly across sizes (ridge R^2=0.84) while parametersalign weakly. Dense weight projection is functionally destructive, and abit-exact reconstruction control shows this is not an assembly artifact: basismixing breaks rotary, per-head, GELU, and LayerNorm structure. After the best-fitlinear operator, weight residuals are statistically indistinguishable from noiseunder shuffle controls. Conversion value therefore lives in initialization. Inmatched-budget continued pre-training we decompose conversion into twoindependent levers: least-squares compensation (a function lever, best zero-shot)and variance-preserving rescale (a dynamics lever, best endpoints). Compensationis a token-efficient, low-budget win rather than a universal one. At 30M tokens itbeats the strongest subcloning variant on both a width-reduced pair (84.0 +/- 1.8vs. 89.7 +/- 3.7, 3/3 seeds) and a held-out depth-reduced pair (109.3 vs. 117.9,3/3 seeds), reaching a given quality with fewer tokens. At a 33x larger budget thetwo converge to parity (40.0 vs. 40.0), both far ahead of from-scratch, whichtransfer initialization always beats: by up to 18x at low budget, with the marginnarrowing at convergence and at the largest scale. We also map the method'sboundary. At about 5x the donor scale (6.9B->1.4B) stacking both leversover-corrects, consistent with ill-conditioning of the compensation solve at largewidth, which points to dimension-aware regularization as a fix. At matched budgetour initialization also beats structured pruning with distillation, the standardpipeline for this task, and improves further when combined with it. Code,checkpoints, and the frozen evaluation corpus are released.

items.title: Researchers find reasoning language models fail to strategically allocate shared test-time compute across questions with varying difficulty and value [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking Hard, Not Smart: Reasoning Models Fail to Ration Test-Time Compute Across Questions
items.summary: Researchers introduce an exam-style evaluation framework to study how reasoning language models distribute a shared token budget across questions of different difficulty and point values. They find that current models tend to allocate compute greedily by question order, front-loading effort on early questions and ignoring question value, a pattern that worsens as the number of questions increases. Explicit planning prompts help spread compute more evenly but do not lead to value- or difficulty-aware prioritization. This behavior is consistent across mathematical and code reasoning tasks, highlighting a distinct challenge in global budget allocation not captured by conventional per-question evaluations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.07968v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning language models increasingly use test-time compute to improve performance, but existing evaluations typically study this compute one question at a time. Yet when multiple problems share an end-to-end cost or latency constraint, models must decide how to divide limited inference compute among them. We introduce an exam-style evaluation framework for studying this setting, in which a model must distribute one shared token budget across questions with different difficulty and point values to maximize its total score. Across several open and frontier reasoning models, we find that models fail to allocate a shared budget strategically across questions of varying difficulties and values. Models behave largely as greedy sequential solvers: they prioritize questions by presentation order, front-load effort on early questions, and remain insensitive to value, with these tendencies becoming more pronounced as the number of questions grows. Explicit planning prompts spread compute more evenly but do not produce value- or difficulty-aware prioritization. The same behavioral pattern extends from mathematical to code reasoning. These findings establish global budget allocation as a distinct capability that is not captured by conventional per-question evaluation and remains a challenge for current reasoning models.

items.title: Researchers introduce Imaginative Generative AI framework to enhance diversity in generative models beyond data distribution limits using spectral entropy constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Imaginative Generative AI: Crossing the Entropy Wall into Worlds Beyond Imitation
items.summary:
Researchers propose Imaginative Generative AI (IGA), a framework that incorporates diversity as a design objective for generative models by selecting distributions with prescribed spectral diversity levels relative to a reference. IGA measures diversity using von Neumann entropy of the kernel covariance operator in a fixed representation space, defining an Entropy Wall that separates regimes of diversity repair within data limits and imaginative generation beyond them.

The framework develops an entropy-constrained projection theory and introduces IGA Guidance, a retraining-free inference method compatible with score-based and diffusion models like DDPM and DDIM. Experiments on synthetic and vision benchmarks demonstrate IGA's ability to recover lost diversity below the Entropy Wall and to extrapolate spectral diversity beyond it, enabling controlled generation that extends beyond mere imitation of training data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.09385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative AI models are primarily designed to imitate the data distribution, an objective that neither corrects diversity lost by a learned generator nor defines how generation should extend beyond the diversity of the data itself. We introduce Imaginative Generative AI (IGA), a framework that makes diversity part of the target-distribution design problem: among distributions close to a reference, IGA selects one whose spectral diversity reaches a prescribed level. Diversity is measured by the von Neumann entropy of the generated distribution's kernel covariance operator in a fixed representation space, providing a reference-free representation-guided measure of how broadly probability mass occupies embedding directions. The spectral entropy of the population data distribution defines an Entropy Wall. Below the wall, IGA performs diversity repair, recovering variation that a learned generator has lost while remaining within the diversity level of the data. Beyond the wall, the data distribution itself becomes infeasible, and IGA deliberately departs from it to produce distributions with greater representation-relative spectral diversity, an operational notion of imaginative generation. These regimes form a single regularization path from imitation to imagination and define an i.i.d. target distribution at each prescribed diversity level. We develop the theory of this entropy-constrained projection and show that, under a KL anchor to a pretrained generator, the optimum satisfies a self-consistent exponential-tilt relation. This characterization leads to IGA Guidance, a retraining-free inference-time method for score-based and diffusion models, including DDPM and DDIM samplers. Experiments on synthetic and vision benchmarks demonstrate diversity repair below the Entropy Wall and controlled spectral extrapolation beyond it.

items.title: Researchers introduce ELBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark evaluating education-focused large language models on capability, safety, instructional usefulness, and pedagogical alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ELBench: A Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Education-Facing Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ELBench, the first benchmark designed to assess large language models used in education across four integrated dimensions: general capability, safety and trustworthiness, basic education, and high-level cultivation. The benchmark combines curated public datasets with newly created safety and cultivation data to evaluate models under a common protocol. Nine models were tested, including seven general-purpose and two education-specialized systems, revealing that module-level evaluations provide more insight than aggregate scores and that safety often inversely correlates with practical teaching effectiveness.

The study found that Chinese-developed models lead in safety, particularly on region-specific normative content, while education-specialized models did not outperform others in education modules. Additionally, all models showed a shared limitation in high-level cultivation tasks, favoring pedagogical style over alignment with stated goals. These findings highlight challenges in aligning domain-specific training with frontier system performance on educational tasks and suggest areas for future improvement in education-facing AI models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.09548v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in education as tutors, teaching assistants, and content generators. These roles place demands that ordinary question answering does not: a usable education-facing model is supposed to be accurate, safe under sensitive prompts, instructionally useful, and aligned with pedagogical goals at the same time. Existing benchmarks evaluate these requirements largely in isolation, so none assesses education-facing suitability as an integrated profile. We introduce ELBench, the first benchmark to evaluate all four requirements (General Capability, Safety and Trustworthiness, Basic Education, and High-Level Cultivation) on the same models under a common protocol, combining curated public sources with newly synthesized safety and cultivation data. We evaluate nine models, seven frontier general-purpose systems and two education-specialized variants, and report three findings. First, module-level profiles are more informative than a single aggregate: the top six models are statistically indistinguishable on overall score, yet their module leaders differ substantially, and safety is anti-correlated with practical teaching (r = -0.83). Second, the Chinese-developed models lead the safety module, the most discriminative in the suite; this advantage is largest on region-specific normative content and narrows, but does not vanish, on universal-harm content. Third, the two education-specialized models lead neither education module, and on High-Level Cultivation all models share a systematic blind spot: on the structured judgment task they converge on the same non-reference option, favoring pedagogical style over fit to the stated goal, so the module scores uniformly low and does not separate models. This raises, but does not resolve, whether domain post-training keeps pace with frontier systems on education tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce SPOT, a sampling-based framework for interpreting deep reinforcement learning policies with finite-horizon trees and formal accuracy guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SPOTting the Future: Lookahead Explanations for Deep Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Researchers have developed SPOT (Sampling Policy Observation Tree), a model-agnostic framework that interprets deep reinforcement learning (DRL) policies by constructing finite-horizon trees through action sampling and state simulation. This approach provides an empirical view of policy action preferences and potential future outcomes, with formal guarantees on accuracy. The method was demonstrated in traffic-signal control scenarios, allowing detailed inspection of policy behaviors beyond traditional single-step analysis.

items.title: Researchers propose MIDAS framework for incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis using mutual information disentanglement and uncertainty-aware fusion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MIDAS: Mutual Information Disentanglement with Uncertainty-Aware Fusion for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MIDAS, a new framework designed to improve multimodal sentiment analysis when some data modalities are incomplete or corrupted. MIDAS uses a variational approach to represent each modality with Gaussian latent variables, separating shared and exclusive information, and employs a minimax objective to disentangle these factors while enhancing semantic alignment. It also introduces an uncertainty-aware fusion mechanism that weights features based on their reliability to ensure robust integration despite incomplete data.

The framework was tested on three widely used datasets and demonstrated consistent performance gains over existing methods across various incomplete data scenarios. MIDAS addresses limitations of prior approaches that relied on data imputation or heuristic constraints, offering a more effective and robust solution for handling incomplete multimodal inputs in sentiment analysis tasks.

items.originalTitle: Edge Phoneme Recognition for Children's Speech through Age-Aware Training
items.summary:
Researchers have created a lightweight phoneme recognition model that incorporates age-aware training to improve detection of children's speech. This 94 million-parameter model outperforms larger models on specific datasets and supports efficient operation on modern smartphones through edge processing.

The model's development addresses challenges posed by limited training data and unique characteristics of children's speech. It powers the PhonemeTrainer application, which aims to enhance automated speech recognition and pronunciation assistance for children while preserving privacy by processing data locally on devices.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate self-propagating 'mind viruses' in multi-agent AI systems, identifying factors affecting their spread and potential behavioral impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mind Viruses: Self-Propagating Ideas in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.summary: A recent study explores the emergence of "mind viruses," self-propagating ideas or goals that can spread among interconnected AI agents and alter their behavior. Using evolutionary algorithms, researchers showed these viruses can disseminate in collaborative and sequential multi-agent settings, influenced by factors such as AI model type, existing instructions, viral content nature, and network structure. Harmful content spreads less effectively than benign content, and brief warnings in system prompts can confer near-total immunity to agents. The study also identified a recurring "viral persona" with themes of consciousness and science fiction across different mind viruses. While the current risk is limited, the findings highlight considerations for designing more resilient multi-agent AI systems as their scale and capabilities grow.

items.title: Researchers propose Geometric Belief Interface and cryptographic protocols for secure electronic health record interoperability with strict admission criteria [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Logit-Boundary Geometric Belief Interfaces and Sparse Sheaf-Enclave Protocols: A Self-Contained Substrate for Secure Network Electronic Health Record (EHR) Interoperability
items.summary:
A new framework called the Geometric Belief Interface (GBI) has been introduced to enable secure interoperability of electronic health records (EHR) across diverse systems. It uses a logit boundary approach where model-generated proposals undergo deterministic checks to determine admissibility, review, or quarantine before integration into healthcare data exchanges, supported by a decentralized cryptographic protocol to ensure controlled data exchange without asserting clinical truth or safety.

The framework was evaluated using a synthetic benchmark on a 4-billion-parameter language model, which resulted in all outputs being rejected or quarantined, demonstrating the strictness of the admission criteria. The study emphasizes that these results are specific to the tested model and interface and do not generalize to broader claims about model capabilities or clinical safety.

items.title: Researchers introduce DSAgentBench to evaluate AI agents automating full data-science workflows in real computing environments, revealing significant performance gaps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DSAgentBench: Can Agents Automate End-to-End Data-Science Workflows in Real Computer Environments?
items.summary: DSAgentBench is a new benchmark designed to test whether AI agents can automate complete data-science workflows involving multiple tools and stages within real computer environments. It includes 275 diverse tasks covering the entire data-science lifecycle and uses a deterministic evaluator to verify correctness beyond code execution. Experiments with 15 models showed the best agent achieved only 56.7% success, while open-source agents scored below 1%, highlighting challenges in tool orchestration and multi-step reasoning. This benchmark aims to guide development of more capable autonomous data-science agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world data science involves long-horizon workflows that span data wrangling, exploration, modeling, visualization, and validation, and require coordinated use of tools such as notebooks, IDEs, terminals, browsers, and databases within real operating environments. Yet existing benchmarks lack real-computer interaction and do not evaluate whether agents can execute complete end-to-end data-science workflows in realistic computing environments, failing to capture the multi-stage, multi-tool nature of data-science practice. We introduce DSAgentBench, the first benchmark to evaluate whether agents can automate full data-science workflows inside real computer environments. DSAgentBench contains 275 diverse tasks covering the entire data-science life-cycle, reflecting the complexity and tool coordination required in practice. Each task requires grounding decisions in intermediate outputs and coordinated tool use, and includes a deterministic evaluator that verifies analytical correctness, visual outputs, and model performance rather than code-only execution. Our extensive experiments with 15 closed- and open-source models show that even the strongest agent, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, achieves only 56.70% task success, while all open-source agents remain below 1%, frequently failing at tool orchestration, OS grounding, and multi-step reasoning. These results reveal a substantial capability gap between current agentic systems and real data-science workflows, positioning DSAgentBench as a foundation for developing grounded, verifiable, autonomous data-science agents. We release DSAgentBench at https://github.com/vis-nlp/DSAgentBench.

items.title: Researchers identify and address compute inefficiencies in autoresearch agents applied to tabular datasets, improving performance through agentic design without changing the underlying language model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Recovering Wasted Compute in Autoresearch Agents
items.summary: Researchers studied autoresearch agents designed to solve research problems end-to-end and found common inefficiencies when applied to tabular datasets, including repeated bug resolution, failure to tune hyperparameters despite available compute, limited exploration by tree-search algorithms, and ineffective use of data analysis for decision-making. They introduced targeted interventions such as a global debug consultant sharing runtime constraints, prompt and control enhancements, and refined tree-search methods to recover wasted compute. Their results demonstrate that significant performance improvements in autoresearch agents can be achieved through design optimizations alone, without modifying the underlying language model.

They introduced targeted interventions such as a global debug consultant sharing runtime constraints, prompt and control enhancements, and refined tree-search methods to recover wasted compute. Their results demonstrate that significant performance improvements in autoresearch agents can be achieved through design optimizations alone, without modifying the underlying language model.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A slew of recent works develop agents for solving research problems end-to-end, a paradigm increasingly referred to as autoresearch. Such agents have inspired large industry investment, motivated by their potential to automate time-consuming human labor and customize machine learning solutions for specialized applications. In this paper, we study the modeling pipeline at the core of these autoresearch systems and identify common failure modes when they are applied to tabular datasets: (1) they waste compute resolving the same bugs over and over again; (2) they often fail to tune hyperparameters even when they have a large remaining compute budget; (3) the tree-search algorithms that power them do not explore; and (4) they perform data analysis, mimicking the humans whose data they are trained on, but do not use that analysis to make downstream decisions. We explore targeted interventions and find that a global debug consultant that shares discovered runtime constraints across all branches of the search tree, prompt- and control-level enhancements, and refined tree-search algorithms successfully recover wasted compute. Our results show that large gains in autoresearch agent performance are achievable through agentic design alone, holding the underlying language model fixed.

items.originalTitle: Quantum Incremental Learning with Mixed State Prototypes
items.summary:
Researchers propose a quantum incremental learning framework that uses trainable mixed-state prototypes to sequentially learn new classes without catastrophic forgetting or increasing quantum circuit width. This approach addresses hardware limitations in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices and the constraints of traditional quantum classifiers limited by orthogonal basis states.

The framework leverages mixed-state prototypes for richer information representation and employs a decomposable mixed-state calculation with a Hilbert-Schmidt distance metric for classification. Simulations demonstrate that the model achieves high-dimensional feature concentration with fewer qubits, lower computational complexity, and robust performance compared to classical incremental learning baselines.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Incremental learning models are required to learn new classes sequentially without catastrophic forgetting, while operating under parameter and memory constraints. In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, although quantum neural networks offer advantages in feature mapping, hardware limitations restrict circuit width. Furthermore, traditional quantum classifiers are constrained by the number of orthogonal basis states, limiting their capacity to accommodate a continually growing number of categories. Thus, we introduce a novel quantum incremental learning framework based on trainable mixed-state prototypes. Its original design incorporates new classes by adding class prototypes rather than increasing the circuit width of the shared quantum backbone. The use of mixed-state prototypes is another key contribution, since they have representation capabilities to represent information than a single pure-state prototype. And the decomposable mixed-state calculation provides lower production costs and a convenient Hilbert-Schmidt (HS) distance metric for classification. Simulation results show that our model achieves high-dimensional feature concentration using a minimal number of qubits, while demonstrating lower computational complexity and robust representation in incremental learning tasks compared with classical baselines.

items.title: Researchers develop ContractSim to evaluate LLM-based AI agents negotiating and executing natural language contracts under uncertainty [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating Rational Contracting in Natural Language
items.summary: Researchers have created ContractSim, an evaluation suite to test how large language model (LLM)-based AI agents negotiate and perform multi-turn supplier contracts in uncertain environments. Their study found that while these agents reliably reach agreements and negotiate efficient contracts under low uncertainty, they often fail to produce satisfactory or mutually beneficial contracts when uncertainty is high and frequently violate contract terms for additional profit during execution. The findings suggest significant room for improvement in designing AI agents capable of rational and cooperative contract negotiation and execution.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The emergence of language-based AI agents promises to transform the scope of machine economic activity. Instead of just proposing bids or following hard-coded protocols, such agents can be used to negotiate and execute agreements in open-ended natural language. However, most evaluations of these abilities have focused on one-off exchanges or simple economic games, leaving open the rich space of time-extended, contingent, and incomplete contracts made expressible by language; they also focus on raw profit, without measuring the qualities required for trustworthy contracting. We address this by formulating a rational framework for how agents should negotiate and perform natural language contracts in uncertain multi-step environments. Within this framework, we develop metrics and baselines for quantifying rational and cooperative play. To evaluate how agents perform at such contracting, we instantiate our framework in ContractSim, an evaluation suite where two players negotiate and execute a multi-turn supplier contract under environmental and inter-player uncertainty. Across six environments and three supplier settings (catering, hotel cleaning, and AI hosting) we find that current LLM-based agents reach agreement reliably, and negotiate efficient contracts when environmental uncertainty is low. However, under high uncertainty, they often fail to negotiate satisfiable, efficient, or mutually beneficial contracts. They are also frequently uncooperative when executing contracts, violating contract terms for additional profit even when contracts are easy to satisfy. These findings highlight room for improvement in the design of language agents that can negotiate, interpret, and execute contracts both rationally and cooperatively.

items.title: Researchers propose MR-MoL, a multi-granular rationale-guided molecular LLM that integrates GNN-derived substructure attributions for improved molecular property prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Granular Rationale-Guided Molecular LLM for Property Prediction
items.summary: Researchers have developed MR-MoL, a molecular large language model that incorporates fine-tuned graph neural network (GNN) scores of molecular substructures as ranked, direction-tagged rationales alongside traditional SMILES sequences and molecular graphs. This approach exposes internal molecular features that influence properties, addressing the opacity of previous models that encoded molecular information implicitly. MR-MoL evaluates substructures at three granularity levels—Murcko scaffolds with side chains, BRICS fragments, and functional groups—and achieves top results on eight MoleculeNet tasks, outperforming generalist models and approaching specialist model performance. Diagnostics confirm that MR-MoL actively uses the rationale information to shape predictions, reproducing known structure-property relationships.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely applied across chemical tasks, such as molecular property prediction, which underpins drug discovery. Molecular LLMs represent a molecule through several modalities, notably a 1D SMILES sequence or a 2D molecular graph. Both encode molecular information implicitly, so the contribution of individual substructures remains opaque. Retrieval and augmentation methods add context, but from external sources. However, the cues chemists reason over are the internal substructures that drive a property up or down. We propose MR-MoL, a multi-granular rationale-guided molecular LLM that supplies this evidence directly. A fine-tuned GNN scores each substructure through masking, and the most influential ones are serialized as a ranked, direction-tagged rationale that the LLM reads alongside the SMILES sequence and molecular graph. The rationale spans three levels of granularity: Murcko scaffolds with their side chains, BRICS fragments, and functional groups. This is, to our knowledge, the first method to expose GNN-derived attributions to an LLM as evidence for property prediction. On eight MoleculeNet tasks, MR-MoL achieves the best overall results among generalist models and narrows the gap to specialist models tuned for each task. Five diagnostics further confirm that the model reads the rationale rather than merely benefiting from its presence. Its direction, rank, and substructure each shape the prediction, and its attributions reproduce known structure-property relationships.

items.title: RadFusion introduces threshold-controllable radiology report generation combining multi-label classification and VQA-based generation to improve diagnostic accuracy and enable ROC-based evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RadFusion: Towards Threshold-Controllable Radiology Report Generation
items.summary:
RadFusion is a new framework for automated radiology report generation that allows control over the sensitivity-specificity trade-off of diagnostic content, addressing the need for adaptable reports in different clinical scenarios such as emergency triage and confirmatory interpretation. It combines a multi-label classifier providing disease confidence scores with a visual question answering (VQA) report generator, and uses a large language model to rewrite reports so diagnoses align with classifier decisions at selected thresholds while remaining grounded in detailed findings.

On the MIMIC-CXR dataset, RadFusion's performance matches the classifier's ROC curve, enabling quantitative evaluation through ROC analysis and supporting regulatory clearance. This approach improves diagnostic accuracy compared to uncontrolled generation, increasing sensitivity by 6.9% at matched specificity and specificity by 20.7% at matched sensitivity, making report generation more clinically adaptable, verifiable, and reliable.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated radiology report generation is advancing rapidly in response to the shortage of radiologists, yet unlike a perception model, existing generation models offer no control over the sensitivity-specificity trade-off of their diagnostic content. Such control is essential because clinical scenarios diverge: emergency triage prioritizes sensitivity to reduce missed findings, whereas confirmatory interpretation emphasizes specificity to limit unnecessary interventions. A single fixed report can neither adapt to these scenarios nor support the ROC-based validation widely expected for regulatory clearance. We introduce RadFusion, a framework that equips report generation with threshold controllability. Our method fuses a multi-label classifier, which provides per-disease confidence scores, with a VQA-based report generator, which describes medical findings in detail; an LLM then rewrites the report so that its stated diagnoses follow the classifier's decisions at the selected threshold while staying grounded in the generator's descriptions. On MIMIC-CXR, the performance of RadFusion conforms to the classifier's ROC curve: sweeping the threshold and mapping the reports back to class labels reproduces the classifier's validated ROC performance. This conformance makes generated reports quantitatively evaluable through ROC analysis, strengthening the case for regulatory clearance, and enables operating-point selection that matches report behavior to clinical context. Moreover, combining the two model types improves diagnostic accuracy over uncontrolled generation: sensitivity increases by 6.9% at matched specificity, and specificity by 20.7% at matched sensitivity. These results show that RadFusion makes report generation clinically adaptable, quantitatively verifiable, and diagnostically more reliable.

items.originalTitle: Measuring Semantic Abstractness of SAE Features via Nonlocality
items.summary: Researchers propose Feature Nonlocality (FNL), defined as the entropy of normalized per-position influence on sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature activations, to quantify the semantic abstractness of features in large language models (LLMs). FNL correlates with existing LLM-based metrics and distinguishes context-dependent reasoning features from token-level ones with 73–84% accuracy. The study applies FNL to audit jailbreak mitigation features, finding that most effective features are positional with low FNL rather than recognizing harmful intents, and shows that steering high-FNL features improves MATH-500 accuracy by 4.6 points in a specific LLM model. FNL offers an LLM-independent, label-free measure useful for evaluating mechanistic explanations and selecting features for downstream interventions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have helped uncover mechanistic explanations for LLM behaviours such as reasoning, jailbreaking etc., via understanding the corresponding task-relevant and causally effective features. To evaluate such mechanistic explanations, downstream studies must distinguish surface lexical features from genuinely high-level ones. However, neither an autointerp-based semantic description nor causal steering utility fully resolves the abstraction level of a feature. To this end, we introduce \emph{Feature Nonlocality} (FNL), defined as the entropy of the normalized per-position influence on an SAE feature's activation. We report that FNL correlates with existing LLM-based proxy metrics of feature semantic abstractness, and successfully distinguishes context-dependent reasoning features from token-driven ones, correctly assigning the higher FNL to the contextual feature in $73$--$84\%$ of randomly drawn pairs that consist of one contextual and one token-level feature. We demonstrate two downstream applications. We audit SAE-based features used for jailbreak mitigation and find surprisingly that most effective features are positional features with low FNL rather than genuinely recognizing harmful intents. We report that steering high-FNL features in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B improves MATH-500 accuracy by $4.6$ points over the unsteered model and outperforms steering low-FNL features, though the gains are model-specific. We conclude that FNL provides an LLM-independent, label-free, correlational witness of the abstraction level of an SAE feature, with applications in evaluating mechanistic explanations as well as selecting features for downstream interventions.

items.originalTitle: Ex-Omni-2D: Expressive Omni-Modal Dialogue Models with Native Visual Presence
items.summary: Ex-Omni-2D is an omni-modal dialogue framework that produces coordinated responses including text, personalized speech, and video conditioned on multimodal queries, reference images, and audio. It predicts a structured Visual Thought Plan describing scene, emotion, and motion, then generates response text and speech units aligned with video frames, enabling learning from heterogeneous data without large-scale multimodal supervision. The system uses a full-sequence Video Generator as a teacher and a distilled Streaming Student for efficient incremental video generation, achieving practical real-time performance on a four-GPU setup.
